source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 2026): only designer; worked with founders, engineers and ops/marketing; Jan–Apr 2026; Yelo's earlier app (Old page) was live; its home was too crowded, social felt bolted on, dated look; the founders picked among directions A–D; B's layout went forward because booking stays first, combined with A; reaction counts were dropped because they felt tacky and few people would tap them (they came from an earlier iMessage-based version where people reacted to ride requests); feed-card changes were his own judgment; home + feed, search + map, ride options and onboarding are live; vehicles sketched first, then modelled and iterated with Gemini, generated together for consistency; no usage numbers. Takeaways he chose: old habits inform design; booking first, social second; simplifying a crowded home.

fields.description: Redesigning a live campus ride-share app: booking first, social second.
fields.intro: Yelo is a student-only campus ride-share. As the only designer, I redesigned its live rider app, from the home screen to ride options and sign-up.
fields.summary: How might we keep a social ride-share social without getting in the way of booking a ride?
fields.overview: Yelo’s earlier app was already live. I redesigned the rider app with the founders, the engineers and the wider team, and the redesign is now live.
fields.impact: The redesign is live: home, search, ride options and sign-up.

sections.title: Problem
sections.heading: A crowded home on a live app
content: Yelo’s earlier app was already live. Its home packed hotness scores, tickers, promos and events around “Where to?”.

bullets: **Too crowded:** too much competed with booking a ride.
**Social felt bolted on:** it didn’t connect to getting a ride.
**Dated look:** the visual design felt old.

gallery.alt: Yelo’s earlier home screen with a dark photo header, Ride and Drive toggle, a ticker, and place cards with hotness scores and badges
The redesigned Yelo home: Where to? search at the top and feed cards for where people are headed

content.caption: Before: the earlier home. After: the redesign.

sections.title: Four directions
sections.heading: Four ways to lay out home
content: I started on paper with one question: what’s the best way to show that a place is popular?

content.alt: Hand-drawn wireframes of the Yelo home screen and three ways to mark a popular location
content.caption: Early sketches: three ways to mark a popular place.

content: From there I narrowed the explorations to four directions on the same header:

bullets: **A:** feed first, with search in a bottom sheet.
**C:** the feed as chat bubbles with reactions.
**D:** a ranked list of popular places.

content.alt: Four Yelo home screen directions side by side: feed first, search first, chat bubbles, ranked list
content.caption: A, B, C and D.

content: The founders chose the direction. V1 combined two of them:

bullets: **B’s layout:** booking stays first, so search sits at the top.
**A’s live row:** “Someone is searching for a ride…”.

**No reaction counts:** they came from an earlier version that ran through iMessage, where people reacted to each other’s ride requests. In the app they felt a bit tacky, and we didn’t think many people would tap them.

content.alt: Yelo V1 home: search first, a Someone is searching for a ride row, and feed cards without reaction counts
content.caption: V1: B’s layout with A’s live row, and no reaction counts.

sections.title: Feed card
sections.heading: A card that says who and where
content: From there I refined the feed card one change at a time:

bullets: “Someone you may know” became a MUTUAL tag.
Labels for each kind of signal (HEADED TO, TRENDING SEARCH, GOT TICKETS) came in one at a time.

content.alt: Four Yelo home screens showing the feed card change: Ride to cards, Headed to cards with initials, a MUTUAL tag, and labelled cards
content.caption: Left to right: V1, “Headed to”, the MUTUAL tag, labelled cards.

sections.title: Ride options
sections.heading: Ride options you can picture
content: The ride sheet went from Exclusive vs. Shared with a seat stepper, to ETA first, to four named vehicle classes with one tag each.

content.alt: Three versions of the Yelo ride sheet: Exclusive or Shared with a seat stepper, ETA first, and named vehicle classes with 3D cars
content.caption: Left to right: Exclusive or Shared, ETA first, named classes.

content: I sketched the vehicles first, then used Gemini to model and iterate on them. Generating all five in one image kept them consistent.

content.alt: Five yellow 3D vehicles in a row: sedan, SUV, golf cart with a flag, van and bus
content.caption: Car, Big Car, Cart, Mini Bus and bus.

bullets: **Sign-up** verifies student status with a school Google or Microsoft account.
**Permissions** each come with a reason, like “See where your friends are headed”.

gallery.alt: Yelo sign-up screen: Claim your student status with Continue with Google or Microsoft
Yelo permissions screen with a reason for notifications, location and contacts
Yelo map tab with event posters stacked across campus and event cards below

content.caption: Student verification, permissions and the event map.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: What shipped and what I learned
content: The redesign is live: home and feed, search and map, ride options and sign-up. I don’t have usage numbers for it.

bullets: **Old habits inform design.** How people used the iMessage version shaped what we kept and what we dropped.
**Booking first, social second.** Social signals only help if they don’t slow down getting a ride.
**Redesigning a live app is mostly removing things.**
